title: Decorator Pattern
tagline: Stack behaviours on an object at runtime by wrapping it in a chain of decorators — no subclass explosion, no modification of the original class.

sections.content:
Imagine you need to add logging, caching, authentication checking, and rate-limiting to a `UserService`. The naive approach is inheritance: `LoggingUserService extends UserService`, then `CachingLoggingUserService extends LoggingUserService`, then `AuthCachingLoggingUserService extends CachingLoggingUserService`. With just four features you already have a brittle hierarchy — and if some objects need only logging, some need only caching, and some need all four in different orders, you need 2⁴ = 16 subclasses to cover every combination. Add a fifth feature and that doubles to 32. This is the **subclass explosion** problem, and it is one of the oldest pain points in object-oriented design.

**The Decorator pattern** is the structural solution. Instead of baking behaviours into subclasses, you wrap an object in a series of thin **decorator** objects, each adding exactly one behaviour and then delegating to the next layer in the chain. The decorated object and every decorator implement the same interface, so the client cannot tell the difference between the raw object and a fully wrapped stack. You compose behaviour by nesting: `new CachingDecorator(new LoggingDecorator(new UserService()))`. To add rate-limiting, you wrap the outside: `new RateLimitDecorator(new CachingDecorator(...))`. To remove logging, you remove that layer. No class is ever modified.

This is not an academic pattern. It is the structural backbone of **Express and Koa middleware chains**, **Python's `@decorator` syntax**, **Java Spring AOP annotations** (`@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@Retryable`), **NestJS interceptors, guards, and pipes**, and virtually every HTTP client library that supports request/response interception. Understanding the Decorator pattern means understanding how these frameworks actually work under the hood.

sections.caption: The Component interface is implemented by both the ConcreteComponent and the BaseDecorator. All concrete decorators extend BaseDecorator, which stores a reference to the wrapped Component. This is the entire structural skeleton of the pattern.

sections.title: The Coffee Shop Order
sections.content:
Walk into a speciality coffee shop and order a plain espresso — that is your **Concrete Component**, the base object with its own inherent behaviour (it costs $2 and describes itself as 'Espresso'). Now ask for milk: the barista does not make a brand-new drink from scratch; they take the existing espresso and add a thin wrapper of milk — a `MilkDecorator`. The result still behaves like a coffee drink (same interface: it has a cost and a description) but cost is now $2.50 and description is 'Espresso, Milk'.

Add caramel syrup: another thin wrapper goes around the milk-wrapped espresso. Add whipped cream: yet another wrapper. At the register, asking `getCost()` unwinds the chain outward-to-inward: whip adds its $0.60 and asks the caramel layer for its cost, which adds $0.75 and asks the milk layer, which adds $0.50 and asks the espresso, which returns $2.00. The total $3.85 emerges from the chain.

The crucial insight: at no point did the barista create a `WhippedCaramelMilkEspresso` class. Any topping in any order is handled by the same three decorator types. That is why N toppings require only N decorator classes rather than 2^N subclasses.

sections.title: The Problem in Detail: Why Inheritance Fails
sections.content:
To fully appreciate the Decorator pattern you need to feel the pain it replaces. Consider a `DataSource` abstraction for reading and writing data. The base implementation reads and writes raw bytes to a file. Now you need some combinations of these behaviours on top: **encryption** (for GDPR compliance), **compression** (for network bandwidth), and **checksum validation** (for data integrity).

With inheritance you need:
- `FileDataSource` (base)
- `EncryptedDataSource extends FileDataSource`
- `CompressedDataSource extends FileDataSource`
- `ChecksumDataSource extends FileDataSource`
- `EncryptedCompressedDataSource extends EncryptedDataSource`
- `EncryptedChecksumDataSource extends EncryptedDataSource`
- `CompressedChecksumDataSource extends CompressedDataSource`
- `EncryptedCompressedChecksumDataSource extends EncryptedCompressedDataSource`

That is 8 classes for 3 features. With 4 features it is 16. Each subclass duplicates logic from siblings. Adding a fourth feature requires modifying or adding to every leaf subclass. Changing the order of operations (encrypt-then-compress vs. compress-then-encrypt) requires another set of subclasses.

Furthermore, **inheritance binds at compile time**. You cannot decide at runtime, based on a config file, whether to apply encryption. With decorators you decide at wiring time — and different environments can wire the same `FileDataSource` with different decorator stacks.

The Decorator pattern also respects the **Open/Closed Principle**: classes are open for extension (by wrapping) but closed for modification. You never touch `FileDataSource` to add encryption — you write `EncryptionDecorator` as a separate class.

flowchart TD

    B --> C["5 features via inheritance\n32 subclasses"]
    D["3 features via Decorator\n3 decorator classes"] --> E["4 features via Decorator\n4 decorator classes"]

sections.caption: Subclass count grows exponentially with inheritance (2^N) but only linearly with decorators (N classes). At 5 features the difference is 32 subclasses versus 5 decorator classes.

sections.title: The Four Participants: A Structural Deep Dive
sections.content:
The GoF Decorator pattern has four participants. Understanding each precisely is essential for implementing the pattern correctly.

**1. Component Interface** — The contract that both the real object and all decorators implement. This is what the client code depends on. It should be a narrow interface (ideally 1-3 methods) — the wider the interface, the more methods every decorator must implement. In JavaScript/TypeScript this is often a class or interface; in dynamically typed languages it is implicit (duck typing).

**2. Concrete Component** — The real, base object that does the actual work when no decoration intervenes. It has no knowledge of decorators. It simply implements the Component Interface with its core behaviour. Examples: a raw file I/O class, a plain `fetch` call, a database query executor.

**3. Base Decorator** — An abstract class that also implements the Component Interface and holds a reference (called `wrappee` or `wrapped` or `component`) to another Component. Its default implementation of every method simply delegates to the wrappee unchanged. This is the structural key: by delegating, the chain passes the call forward. Concrete decorators extend this class and override only the methods they want to intercept.

**4. Concrete Decorators** — Extend the Base Decorator. Each adds one specific behaviour, either before the delegation call (pre-processing, like checking auth), after the delegation call (post-processing, like logging the response), or both (like a timer that records start time before and elapsed time after). A concrete decorator may also add its own state — for example, a `CachingDecorator` stores a cache map.

**The missing participant — Client** — assembles the stack by wrapping a Concrete Component in decorators. The client treats the entire stack as a single Component. This wiring is usually done in a Dependency Injection container, a factory function, or an application bootstrap file.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Notice that `deluxe` and `reordered` have the same cost but different descriptions. Order of decoration matters when each layer's behaviour depends on the result of the inner layer. For cost (purely additive) order is irrelevant; for operations like encrypt-then-compress vs. compress-then-encrypt the order critically affects the result.

sections.title: Cross-Cutting Concerns: The Real-World Use Case
sections.content:
The coffee analogy is illustrative, but the pattern's dominant real-world application is **cross-cutting concerns** in software systems. A cross-cutting concern is a behaviour that spans multiple modules and cannot be cleanly encapsulated in any one of them: logging, authentication, caching, transaction management, error retry, rate-limiting, and performance monitoring.

Consider a Node.js service with five different service classes: `UserService`, `OrderService`, `ProductService`, `PaymentService`, and `InventoryService`. Each needs:
- **Logging**: record what method was called, with what arguments, and what it returned
- **Caching**: memoise results keyed by arguments to avoid redundant database calls
- **Authentication**: verify the caller has the right role before the method executes

Without decorators, you write this logic three times in every service class — 15 copies of cross-cutting code across five services. When the logging format changes you update 5 classes. When caching strategy changes, 5 more.

With decorators, you write `LoggingDecorator`, `CachingDecorator`, and `AuthDecorator` once each. You then wire each service with the appropriate stack in your DI container or factory:

```
UserService    → Auth → Cache → Log → real UserService
OrderService   → Auth → Log  → real OrderService   (no cache needed)
PaymentService → Auth → real PaymentService         (no cache, no extra logging)
```

Each concern is implemented once, tested once, and applied selectively. This is the Open/Closed Principle in practice: you extend each service's behaviour without modifying the service class itself.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: Study the wiring order carefully: `Auth → Cache → Log → UserService`. On a read, Auth passes through, Cache checks its store, if miss it calls Log which logs then calls the real service. On a write, Auth enforces the role, Cache invalidates, Log records the call. Each decorator has exactly one responsibility and zero knowledge of the others. Swap cache and log positions and you change whether cache misses are logged — without editing any class.

sections.title: Decorator vs. Inheritance vs. Strategy: Know the Difference
sections.content:
Students often confuse Decorator with related patterns. Here is a precise comparison:

**Decorator vs. Inheritance** — Inheritance adds behaviour statically at compile time for a specific class. You cannot inherit from an object you do not own, and you cannot unapply behaviour at runtime. Decoration adds behaviour dynamically at runtime for any object implementing the interface. A Decorator can wrap objects of classes it has never heard of, as long as they implement the interface. In statically typed languages, inheritance also suffers from the fragile base class problem: changes to the parent silently affect all children.

**Decorator vs. Strategy** — Strategy changes the core algorithm of an object (swapping out *how* it does its job). Decorator keeps the core algorithm and wraps additional behaviour around it (adding *what else* happens). A sorting service might use a `QuickSortStrategy` or a `MergeSortStrategy` — different core algorithms. A `LoggingDecorator` around it adds logging but never changes how sorting works.

**Decorator vs. Proxy** — Structurally nearly identical: both wrap an object and implement its interface. The intent differs. A Proxy controls *access* (lazy initialisation, remote delegation, access control, caching as access control). A Decorator adds *behaviour* without restricting access. The line blurs in practice — a caching decorator behaves like a proxy; many frameworks use the terms interchangeably.

**Decorator vs. Adapter** — An Adapter translates one interface into another (solving an incompatibility). A Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour (enhancing compatibility). Structure is similar; intent is completely different.

**Decorator vs. Composite** — Composite trees represent part-whole hierarchies where containers and leaves share an interface. Decorators also wrap objects sharing an interface but add behaviour rather than managing children. The structural similarity is why both patterns appear in the same category, but their purposes are orthogonal.

sections.title: The Decorator Pattern in Real Frameworks
sections.content:
Understanding how frameworks implement this pattern makes the abstractions concrete:

**Express.js middleware** is textbook Decorator. Each middleware function receives `(req, res, next)` and must call `next()` to delegate to the next middleware — the analog of `super.operation()`. The middleware stack is assembled in order at application startup: `app.use(helmet())` wraps every route with security headers; `app.use(compression())` wraps with gzip. Each adds behaviour and delegates via `next()`.

**Python decorators** (`@functools.lru_cache`, `@login_required`, `@retry`) are function-level Decorators. They wrap a function in another function that adds behaviour before/after invoking the original. `@lru_cache` is a CachingDecorator for functions; `@login_required` in Django is an AuthDecorator. The `@` syntax is sugar for `view = login_required(view)`.

**Java Spring AOP** uses `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@Retryable`. Spring generates a proxy at runtime that wraps your service bean in a decorator stack corresponding to your annotations. `@Transactional` begins a database transaction before your method and commits/rolls back after — exactly a Decorator. `@Cacheable` caches the return value — another Decorator. The fact that Spring calls these aspects and uses AOP terminology does not change the structural pattern.

**NestJS interceptors** implement `NestInterceptor` and wrap the handler call observable — each interceptor in the pipeline is a Decorator. Guards and pipes are also structural decorators that run before handler execution.

**Axios/fetch interceptors**: `axios.interceptors.request.use(fn)` and `axios.interceptors.response.use(fn)` add decorators to the request/response pipeline — auth headers, error normalisation, logging.

**Java I/O streams** are the canonical GoF example: `new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(file)))` chains three decorators. `BufferedReader` adds buffering around `InputStreamReader` which adds charset decoding around `FileInputStream`.

sections.caption: Express middleware is a Decorator chain. Each middleware wraps the next. Request flows in, response flows out, each layer adding its behaviour. This is identical to the Decorator pattern — just named 'middleware'.

sections.title: Implementation Pitfalls and Edge Cases
sections.content:
Several subtle problems arise when implementing Decorators in practice:

**Forgetting to delegate** — The most common bug. If a concrete decorator overrides a method and does its work but forgets to call `super.operation()` (or `this._wrapped.operation()`), the chain is broken. Every layer below that decorator never executes. This is particularly dangerous in large stacks where the missing call is not immediately obvious.

**Wide component interfaces** — If the Component Interface has 20 methods, every decorator must implement all 20, even if it only cares about one. The Base Decorator class mitigates this by providing default delegation for all methods, but it still creates boilerplate. Narrow interfaces (ideally 1-3 methods) make decorators far more practical.

**Type identity loss** — After decoration, `instanceof ConcreteComponent` returns false. If any code checks the concrete type (violating Liskov), the decorator stack breaks it. Decorators work only when clients depend exclusively on the Component Interface.

**Stack order matters for non-commutative operations** — Encrypt-then-compress and compress-then-encrypt produce different results and potentially different security properties. Logging before caching means every call is logged; logging after caching means only cache misses are logged. Teams must document and enforce the intended stack order.

**State in decorators** — Stateful decorators (like `CachingDecorator` with its `Map`) can introduce unexpected sharing if the same decorator instance is wrapped around multiple components. Each decorated object should get its own decorator instance unless sharing is intentional.

**Performance overhead** — Each method call traverses every decorator layer. For a 5-layer stack, calling one method involves 5 function calls. In hot paths (tight loops, high-frequency streaming), this overhead can matter. Profile before optimising — in most application code, the overhead is negligible compared to I/O.

sections.label: Example
sections.explanation: The read path reverses the write path automatically because each decorator's `read()` delegates first and then post-processes. `EncryptionDecorator.read()` calls `CompressionDecorator.read()` which calls `FileDataSource.read()` which returns the raw bytes. Then Compression decorates on the way back, then Encryption. This bidirectional chain is a powerful property of the pattern — you get symmetric encode/decode for free from the same structure.

sections.content: **The ES2022/TypeScript Decorator Proposal** introduces `@decorator` syntax as a language feature. It is a different mechanism from the structural Decorator *pattern* — it is a function applied to a class or method at class-definition time by the JavaScript engine. However, the *intent* is identical: `@Injectable()` in Angular wraps the class in DI metadata; `@Transactional()` in TypeORM wraps a method in transaction logic. The pattern and the language feature are distinct but spiritually aligned. When you write `@UseGuards(AuthGuard)` in NestJS, you are applying a Guard decorator that NestJS wraps around your handler — the structural Decorator pattern, expressed through the language's decorator syntax.

**When to use Decorator:**
- You need to add one or more cross-cutting concerns (logging, caching, auth, retry, rate-limiting) to objects independently and in different combinations.
- You cannot or should not modify the class being extended (third-party code, sealed class, violation of Single Responsibility).
- You need runtime flexibility to apply or remove behaviours based on configuration.
- The number of possible feature combinations would cause subclass explosion with inheritance.

**When NOT to use Decorator:**
- The combination of behaviours is always fixed — a single class that has all the logic is simpler and more debuggable.
- You need to add behaviour to the class itself (all instances), not to individual objects — use a subclass or mixin instead.
- The component interface is very wide (many methods) — boilerplate delegation in the Base Decorator becomes burdensome; consider an AOP framework instead.
- Deeply nested stacks (5+) make debugging painful — stack traces show the decorator layers, not the real call site.

**Framework alternatives:** When your language or framework already provides first-class support (Spring AOP, NestJS interceptors, Python decorators, Express middleware), prefer those over hand-rolling the pattern — they provide better tooling, error messages, and interop with the framework's DI system.

items: The **Decorator pattern** solves subclass explosion by composing behaviour at runtime: with N features you need N decorator classes instead of 2^N subclasses.

Every decorator implements the **same interface** as the component it wraps, making the entire stack transparent to the client — the client cannot and should not know whether it is talking to the raw object or a ten-layer stack.
The **Base Decorator** is the structural key: it holds a reference to the wrappee and provides default delegation. Concrete decorators extend it and override only the methods they want to intercept.

**Order of decoration matters** for non-commutative operations: encrypt-then-compress differs from compress-then-encrypt; logging before caching differs from logging after caching. Document and enforce intended stack order.

The pattern is everywhere in real frameworks: **Express middleware**, **Python `@decorators`**, **Spring AOP annotations**, **NestJS interceptors/guards/pipes**, and **Java I/O streams** are all structural Decorators under different names.

The critical implementation rule: **always delegate** by calling `super.method()` or `this._wrapped.method()` inside every overridden method. Forgetting this call silently breaks the entire chain below that decorator.

Use Decorator for **cross-cutting concerns applied selectively and in combination**. Prefer simpler composition when the combination of concerns is fixed, and prefer framework-native solutions (AOP, middleware) when they are available.

quiz.question: With 4 independent features, how many subclasses does an inheritance-based solution need to cover every combination, compared to a Decorator-based solution?
options: Inheritance: 4, Decorator: 16
Inheritance: 16, Decorator: 4
Inheritance: 8, Decorator: 4
Both require the same number of classes
quiz.explanation: Inheritance requires 2^N subclasses to cover every combination of N features (2^4 = 16). Decorator requires only N decorator classes (4) — each feature is one class that can be combined freely at runtime.

quiz.question: Why must every Decorator implement the same interface as the component it wraps?
options: To allow the decorator to access private fields of the component
So that the client can use a decorated object wherever a plain component is expected, without modification
To enable multiple inheritance between decorators
To prevent direct instantiation of the concrete component
quiz.explanation: Implementing the same interface makes the decorator transparent to the client — the client cannot tell whether it holds the raw component or a stack of 10 decorators. This is the Liskov Substitution Principle in action: a decorated object must be substitutable for the undecorated original.

quiz.question: In the stack `new AuthDecorator(new CachingDecorator(new LoggingDecorator(new UserService())))`, when `getUser(42)` is called and results in a cache miss, which layer executes FIRST?
options: LoggingDecorator, because it is closest to the real service
UserService, because it is the concrete component
AuthDecorator, because it is the outermost wrapper
CachingDecorator, because it controls whether the inner layers run
quiz.explanation: AuthDecorator is the outermost layer — the client's direct reference — so its code runs first. It then delegates to CachingDecorator (which checks the cache, gets a miss, and delegates to LoggingDecorator), which delegates to UserService. The outermost decorator always executes first.

quiz.question: What is the role of the Base Decorator class in the pattern?
options: It implements all business logic so concrete decorators do not have to
It holds a reference to the wrappee and provides default delegation — concrete decorators extend it and override only what they need to change
It replaces the Component Interface by providing a richer contract
It prevents any decorated object from being modified after construction
quiz.explanation: The Base Decorator stores the wrappee and provides pure delegation (calling the wrappee) as the default for every method. Concrete decorators extend it, override the methods they care about, add their behaviour, and call super to delegate. Without the Base Decorator, every concrete decorator would need to delegate every method manually.

quiz.question: A CachingDecorator wraps a LoggingDecorator which wraps UserService. You swap the order: LoggingDecorator now wraps CachingDecorator. How does behaviour change?
options: No change — the result is identical regardless of stack order
Cache hits are now logged; previously only cache misses were logged
Logging now only sees cache misses; previously all calls were logged
The swap causes a stack overflow because decorators cannot wrap each other
quiz.explanation: In the original stack (Cache outer, Log inner), a cache hit never reaches LoggingDecorator — Cache returns early from its own store. In the swapped stack (Log outer, Cache inner), Log always runs first for every call, then delegates to Cache. So logging now only captures calls that miss the cache — previously ALL calls were logged.

options: It uses Date.now() which is not accurate enough for timing
It returns a hardcoded string instead of delegating — the entire wrapped chain below this decorator never executes
Decorators cannot have console.log statements
The method should be async to avoid blocking
quiz.explanation: The decorator forgot to call `super.operation()` (which would delegate to the next layer). Without that call, the entire chain below this decorator is silently short-circuited — no inner decorators or the concrete component ever run. This is the most common Decorator implementation bug.

quiz.question: How does the Decorator pattern structurally differ from the Adapter pattern?
options: Decorator uses inheritance; Adapter uses composition
Decorator keeps the same interface and adds behaviour; Adapter changes the interface to match what the client expects
Adapter keeps the same interface; Decorator changes the interface
Both patterns are structurally and intentionally identical
quiz.explanation: A Decorator wraps an object to add behaviour while preserving the same interface — the client sees no difference. An Adapter wraps an object to translate its interface into a different one that the client expects. The structures are similar (both use composition) but the intents are opposite: one preserves the interface, the other changes it.

quiz.question: Which of the following is NOT a real-world application of the Decorator pattern?
options: Express.js middleware pipeline with app.use()
Python @lru_cache and @login_required function decorators
Java Spring @Transactional and @Cacheable annotations
React component props spreading with {...props}
quiz.explanation: React props spreading is a data composition technique, not a structural Decorator. The other three are direct applications: Express middleware is a Decorator chain with next(); Python decorators wrap functions; Spring AOP generates proxy-Decorators for annotated methods.

quiz.question: When should you prefer a simple subclass over the Decorator pattern?
options: When you need to add behaviour to objects of a third-party class you cannot modify
When you need different combinations of behaviours on different objects at runtime
When the combination of behaviours is always fixed and you only have one variant — a subclass is simpler and easier to debug
When the Component Interface has more than three methods
quiz.explanation: If the combination of behaviours is always the same and there is only one variant, a single subclass (or a class that inlines all the logic) is simpler, more readable, and easier to debug than a Decorator stack. Decorator shines when you need flexibility — different combinations for different objects. Fixed-combination scenarios do not benefit from the added complexity.

quiz.question: In Java's `new BufferedReader(new InputStreamReader(new FileInputStream(file)))`, what structural pattern is this?
options: Composite — a tree of part-whole relationships
Decorator — each class wraps the next and adds one behaviour while keeping the Reader interface
Adapter — each class translates a different interface
Proxy — each class controls access to the underlying file
quiz.explanation: This is the canonical GoF Decorator example. FileInputStream is the Concrete Component (raw bytes). InputStreamReader decorates it with charset decoding (adds behaviour: byte-to-char). BufferedReader decorates that with buffering (adds behaviour: line-at-a-time reading). All three implement compatible Reader interfaces, and each adds exactly one responsibility.
